The manipulation of time in the story is very effective and well-balanced. In terms of "story time," the actual present-day action spans only a few minutes—Nora unlocks the door, steps into the hallway, glances into the living room and kitchen, and stops at the foot of the stairs. 

The writer stretches these few minutes by interweaving sensory details (the greenish light, the smell of dust and violets) with compressed summaries of the past twenty years (the mother's death, the overgrown hedge, the sold television). This stretching of the present moment slows the pacing down, mirroring Nora's hesitation and building a quiet, eerie suspense that culminates effectively in the final lines when she smells the fresh soap.
